desc:
You are given intervals, where intervals[i] = [start, end] with start ≤ end. All start values are distinct.

The right neighbour of interval i is the interval j (possibly j = i) with the smallest start that is still ≥ end of interval i. Return an array whose entry i is the index j of the right neighbour of interval i, or -1 when no interval starts at or after intervals[i][1].
hints: Checking every other interval for every interval is O(n²). Think about which question each interval asks: 'what is the first start that is at least my end?'
Sort the start values together with their interval indices. The question is exactly a lower-bound query on that sorted list.
For each interval, run lower_bound(end) over the sorted starts. If the result is past the last element, answer -1; otherwise answer the original index stored with that start.
editorial: Build a list of pairs (start, index) sorted by start; since starts are distinct, the order is unambiguous and the answer of every query is unique. For interval i with end e, the right neighbour is the first pair whose start is ≥ e, i.e. the lower bound of e in the list of starts.

Sorting costs O(n log n) and each of the n lower-bound searches costs O(log n), for O(n log n) overall. Note that an interval can be its own right neighbour when start == end, because its own start is then ≥ its end.
solution:
from bisect import bisect_left

def rightIntervals(intervals):
    order = sorted(range(len(intervals)), key=lambda i: intervals[i][0])
    starts = [intervals[i][0] for i in order]
    out = []
    for s, e in intervals:
        k = bisect_left(starts, e)
        out.append(order[k] if k < len(order) else -1)
    return out
